# Geometric operations {#sec-m2-geometrias}

This chapter is the direct translation of QGIS's **Vector > Geoprocessing** menu into code.
Each operation here is a task you now do by clicking. In code, it is recorded
and can be run again.

```{r}
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# default basemap for mapview(): OpenStreetMap
mapview::mapviewOptions(basemaps = c("OpenStreetMap", "Esri.WorldGrayCanvas", "Esri.WorldImagery"))

crs_trabalho <- 31982   # SIRGAS 2000 / UTM 22S (PR/SC)
```

We will work with real data: the municipalities on the coast of Paraná and Santa Catarina.

```{r}
arquivo <- "dados/brutos/muni_pr_sc.gpkg"

if (!file.exists(arquivo)) {
  # one state at a time, to make clear what each call returns
  muni_pr <- geobr::read_municipality(code_muni = "PR", year = 2022, showProgress = FALSE)
  muni_sc <- geobr::read_municipality(code_muni = "SC", year = 2022, showProgress = FALSE)

  # stacks the two: same columns, one state below the other
  muni <- dplyr::bind_rows(muni_pr, muni_sc)

  sf::st_write(muni, arquivo, quiet = TRUE)
}

muni <- sf::st_read(arquivo, quiet = TRUE) |> sf::st_transform(crs_trabalho)

# standardises the name of the geometry column: each source uses a different name
# ("geom", "geometry", "SHAPE"), and that breaks code written for another dataset
sf::st_geometry(muni) <- "geom"

dim(muni)
names(muni)
```

```{r}
portos <- data.frame(
  nome = c("Paranaguá", "Antonina", "São Francisco do Sul", "Itajaí", "Imbituba"),
  lon  = c(-48.5119, -48.7119, -48.6383, -48.6486, -48.6706),
  lat  = c(-25.5016, -25.4283, -26.2400, -26.9077, -28.2300)
) |>
  sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326) |>
  sf::st_transform(crs_trabalho)
```

## Measures: area, length, perimeter, centroid

```{r}
# perimeter: turns the polygon into a line, measures its length, converts to km.
# in separate steps to make clear what each function returns
muni_linhas    <- sf::st_cast(muni$geom, "MULTILINESTRING")  # polygon -> outline
perimetro_m    <- sf::st_length(muni_linhas)                 # length, in metres
perimetro_km   <- units::set_units(perimetro_m, km)          # metres -> km

muni_area <- muni |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    area_km2 = as.numeric(units::set_units(sf::st_area(geom), km^2)),
    perim_km = as.numeric(perimetro_km)
  )

muni_area |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::slice_max(area_km2, n = 5) |>
  dplyr::select(name_muni, abbrev_state, area_km2, perim_km) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 1))) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r}
centroides <- sf::st_centroid(muni)          # geometric centre
ponto_interno <- sf::st_point_on_surface(muni)  # guaranteed to be inside the polygon
```

`st_centroid()` of a municipality with a very irregular shape, or with islands, may fall **outside**
the polygon. That breaks spatial joins. `st_point_on_surface()` solves this.

## *Buffer*: the area of influence

```{r}
buffer_portos <- sf::st_buffer(portos, dist = 15000)   # 15 km, in metres (projected CRS)

as.numeric(units::set_units(sf::st_area(buffer_portos), km^2)) |> round(1)
```

A visual check before moving on: does the *buffer* cover the expected area around each port?

```{r}
mapview::mapview(buffer_portos) + mapview::mapview(portos)
```

The practical use of an area of influence rarely stops at the drawing: the goal is usually
"which municipalities does it affect". That is answered by comparing the *buffer* with the
`geobr` municipal boundaries, using the same spatial predicates we detail in the next section.
Here is the most common use in advance:

```{r}
buffer_uniao <- sf::st_union(buffer_portos)   # the 5 buffers as a single geometry

municipios_intersecta <- muni[sf::st_intersects(muni, buffer_uniao, sparse = FALSE)[, 1], ]
municipios_toca       <- muni[sf::st_touches(muni, buffer_uniao, sparse = FALSE)[, 1], ]

c(intersecta = nrow(municipios_intersecta), toca_so_pela_borda = nrow(municipios_toca))
```

`st_intersects()` catches any overlap, including a municipality partly covered by the
area of influence. `st_touches()` is stricter: it only counts those that touch exactly at the edge,
without overlapping. For "who is affected by the area of influence", `st_intersects()` is the right
predicate, and it is the one we use from here on.

```{r}
#| label: fig-buffer
#| fig-cap: "Municipalities that intersect each port's 15 km area of influence"
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = muni, fill = "grey97", colour = "grey85", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = municipios_intersecta, fill = "#cfe0ee", colour = "#1a5b8a", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = buffer_portos, fill = "#1a5b8a", alpha = 0.3, colour = "#1a5b8a") +
  geom_sf(data = portos, size = 1.8, colour = "#0d3b5c") +
  geom_sf_text(data = portos, aes(label = nome), size = 2.6, nudge_y = 12000) +
  theme_void(base_size = 10)
```

```{r}
mapview::mapview(municipios_intersecta, col.regions = "#1a5b8a", alpha.regions = 0.3,
                  layer.name = "Affected municipalities") +
  mapview::mapview(buffer_portos, col.regions = "#e07b39", layer.name = "Area of influence") +
  mapview::mapview(portos, layer.name = "Ports")
```

Useful variations:

```{r}
#| eval: false
sf::st_buffer(x, dist = 500, endCapStyle = "FLAT")    # line buffer without a round "cap"
sf::st_buffer(x, dist = -200)                          # negative buffer: shrinks the polygon
sf::st_buffer(x, dist = c(1000, 5000, 10000))          # one radius per feature (vectorised)
```

The negative *buffer* is a practical trick: `st_buffer(area, -100)` removes a 100 m strip from the
edge, useful for discarding edge effects in sampling.

## Spatial relations: who is where

The `st_*` predicate functions answer membership questions. They all return a list
of indices by default, or a logical matrix with `sparse = FALSE`.

```{r}
# which municipalities contain a port? in steps: the comparison matrix,
# then "any TRUE in the row", then the filter
matriz_intersecta <- sf::st_intersects(muni, portos, sparse = FALSE)  # municipalities x ports matrix
tem_porto         <- apply(matriz_intersecta, 1, any)                 # TRUE if the row has any TRUE
com_porto         <- muni[tem_porto, ]

com_porto |> sf::st_drop_geometry() |> dplyr::select(name_muni, abbrev_state)
```

```{r}
# how many ports per municipality (count)
lista_intersecoes <- sf::st_intersects(muni, portos)   # "sparse" form: a list of indices
n_portos_por_muni  <- lengths(lista_intersecoes)        # size of each element of the list

table(n_portos_por_muni)
```

| Predicate | Question |
|:--|:--|
| `st_intersects()` | do they touch in any way? (the most used) |
| `st_within()` | is A inside B? |
| `st_contains()` | does A contain B? |
| `st_touches()` | do they touch only at the edge? |
| `st_crosses()` | do they cross (line × line, line × polygon)? |
| `st_disjoint()` | do they not touch? |
| `st_is_within_distance()` | are they less than X metres apart? |

::: {.callout-tip}
## See the predicates drawn, not just described

The [`sf` cheatsheet](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/sf.pdf) (RStudio/Posit) shows
`st_intersects()`, `st_within()`, `st_contains()` and the other predicates as pairs of shapes
drawn side by side, with the `TRUE`/`FALSE` result of each combination. For beginners,
the visual version sinks in faster than the text description.
:::

```{r}
# municipalities neighbouring Paranaguá (sharing a border). in steps:
pgua         <- muni |> dplyr::filter(name_muni == "Paranaguá")
matriz_toca  <- sf::st_touches(muni, pgua, sparse = FALSE)  # municipalities x 1 (Paranaguá) matrix
eh_vizinho   <- matriz_toca[, 1]                              # single column, becomes a logical vector
vizinhos     <- muni[eh_vizinho, ]

vizinhos |> sf::st_drop_geometry() |> dplyr::pull(name_muni)
```

```{r}
# municipalities less than 50 km from a port. in steps:
matriz_proximo <- sf::st_is_within_distance(muni, portos, dist = 50000, sparse = FALSE)
esta_proximo   <- apply(matriz_proximo, 1, any)
proximos       <- muni[esta_proximo, ]

nrow(proximos)
```

## Spatial join (`st_join`)

It is the spatial equivalent of module 1's `left_join`: instead of matching on a column, it matches on
position.

```{r}
portos_com_muni <- sf::st_join(portos, muni |> dplyr::select(name_muni, abbrev_state, code_muni))

portos_com_muni |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Note that the port gained the municipality's **IBGE code**. That is exactly the key that was missing in
module 1 to join with Census and SIDRA data. This is how the bridge between
spatial data and tabular data is built.

```{r}
#| eval: false
sf::st_join(a, b, join = st_within)         # changes the predicate
sf::st_join(a, b, join = st_nearest_feature) # matches the NEAREST feature (always matches)
sf::st_join(a, b, left = FALSE)              # spatial inner join
```

`st_nearest_feature` is the solution for points that fall slightly outside the polygon: a port
coordinate that landed in the sea, a bus stop on the edge of the census tract.

## Intersection, difference and union

```{r}
# INTERSECTION: clips one layer by the other, keeping the attributes of both
recorte <- sf::st_intersection(muni, buffer_portos |> sf::st_union())

nrow(muni)
nrow(recorte)     # only the municipalities touched, and only the part inside the buffer
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-intersecao
#| fig-cap: "Intersection between municipalities and the ports' areas of influence"
#| fig-height: 4.5
# crops the VIEW to the neighbourhood of the result, with a 20 km margin:
# without it, the map shows the whole PR/SC coast, almost all of it empty
zoom <- sf::st_bbox(sf::st_buffer(sf::st_union(buffer_portos), 20000))

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = muni, fill = "grey97", colour = "grey85", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = recorte, aes(fill = abbrev_state), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(PR = "#1a5b8a", SC = "#e07b39"), name = "State") +
  coord_sf(xlim = zoom[c("xmin", "xmax")], ylim = zoom[c("ymin", "ymax")], expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void(base_size = 10)
```

Intersection is the key operation of the case study: it answers "what part of each census
tract lies inside the catchment". And, with that, how much population is there.

```{r}
#| eval: false
sf::st_difference(a, b)      # what is in A and not in B (inverse clip)
sf::st_sym_difference(a, b)  # what is in one and not in the other
sf::st_union(a)              # dissolves all features into one
sf::st_union(a, b)           # unites two layers
sf::st_combine(a)            # groups without dissolving internal boundaries
```

The difference between `st_union()` and `st_combine()` matters: the first **erases** internal boundaries
(a single polygon); the second just puts them into one *multipart* feature, keeping the
lines. To "dissolve by state", it is `st_union()` inside `group_by`:

```{r}
ufs <- muni |>
  dplyr::group_by(abbrev_state) |>
  dplyr::summarise(geom = sf::st_union(geom), n_muni = dplyr::n())

ufs |> sf::st_drop_geometry()
```

## Distances

```{r}
# port × port distance matrix, in km
d <- sf::st_distance(portos) |>
  units::set_units(km) |>
  as.numeric() |>
  matrix(nrow = nrow(portos), dimnames = list(portos$nome, portos$nome))

round(d, 1)
```

```{r}
# for each municipality, the distance to the nearest port
muni_d <- muni |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    dist_porto_km = round(
      apply(sf::st_distance(sf::st_point_on_surface(geom), portos), 1, min) / 1000, 1),
    porto_proximo = portos$nome[sf::st_nearest_feature(sf::st_point_on_surface(geom), portos)]
  )

muni_d |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::slice_min(dist_porto_km, n = 5) |>
  dplyr::select(name_muni, abbrev_state, porto_proximo, dist_porto_km) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

This is the structure of a rudimentary access indicator: Euclidean distance to the
nearest facility. In module 4 we replace this straight line with **travel time over the
network**, which is what really matters in planning.

## Simplification and performance

Full-resolution IBGE boundaries are heavy. For maps and exploratory operations, it is worth
simplifying:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# geometric simplification (careful: it creates gaps between neighbouring polygons)
muni_simples <- sf::st_simplify(muni, dTolerance = 200, preserveTopology = TRUE)

# geobr already offers the simplified version, which is the best option
geobr::read_municipality(code_muni = "PR", year = 2022, simplified = TRUE)
```

The performance gain is real, but it has a price: the edge loses detail. Compare visually before
choosing the tolerance, overlaying the original and simplified outlines in a single `mapview`:

```{r}
pgua_simples <- sf::st_simplify(pgua, dTolerance = 200, preserveTopology = TRUE)

mapview::mapview(pgua, color = "#1a5b8a", col.regions = NA, lwd = 3,
                  layer.name = "Original") +
  mapview::mapview(pgua_simples, color = "#e07b39", col.regions = NA, lwd = 2,
                    layer.name = "Simplified (200 m)")
```

Zoom into an inlet on the coast: with `dTolerance = 200` the difference is already visible to the naked eye,
especially on the most indented stretches of the coastline.

Three habits that solve almost every slowness problem:

1. Filter **before** operating: crop the study area when reading (`query`, `wkt_filter`).
2. Use the simplified boundaries to visualise and the full ones only to measure.
3. Write intermediate results to `.gpkg` and read from there. Do not recompute on every render.

::: {.callout-note}
## `duckspatial`: when the dataset does not fit in memory

For spatial operations on very large datasets, `duckspatial` exposes DuckDB's spatial
extension with `dplyr` syntax, in the same spirit as module 1's `duckplyr`: the operation runs in the
database and only the result comes back to R.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(duckdb); library(duckspatial)

con <- duckdb::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
duckspatial::ddbs_install(con); duckspatial::ddbs_load(con)

duckspatial::ddbs_write_vector(con, muni, "muni")
duckspatial::ddbs_read_vector(con, "SELECT name_muni, ST_Area(geom) AS area FROM muni LIMIT 5")
```

It pays off from a few hundred thousand features upwards; below that, `sf` is simpler and
fast enough.
:::
